opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot. The short answer is: it's really hard to assess, and I don't think we have good tools for it yet.

When you look at systems like DALL-E or Stable Diffusion, the outputs can be stunning. You type in "an astronaut riding a horse" and you get this beautiful, coherent image. It's tempting to conclude that the system must understand what astronauts are, what horses are, and how riding works. But producing a plausible image isn't the same as having a causal model of the world.

One way I like to probe this is to look at the failures, because they're often more revealing than the successes. If you ask for "a horse riding an astronaut," these systems frequently give you the astronaut on the horse anyway. That tells you the model has learned strong statistical associations between those concepts and typical configurations, but it isn't really composing the meaning of the sentence. Similarly, they often struggle with counting, with spatial relations like "the red cube to the left of the blue sphere," or with negation. Ask for "a room with no elephants" and you might get an elephant. Those are exactly the kinds of things a causal or compositional model of the world should handle easily.

So my approach is to design targeted tests. Rather than relying on aggregate benchmarks, which models can do well on by exploiting shortcuts, you construct cases that systematically vary one thing at a time: swap the roles, change the relations, introduce unusual combinations unlikely to appear in the training data. If the system really has an abstract understanding, it should generalize to those. If it's mostly pattern-matching over its training distribution, it'll break in revealing ways.

I'd also say we have to be careful about our own tendency to anthropomorphize. Humans are very good at reading understanding into things. When an image looks right, we fill in the reasoning ourselves. That's why I think the field needs more rigorous, cognitively inspired evaluation, borrowing from how developmental psychologists test infants or how cognitive scientists test animals, where you can't just ask the subject what it understands. You have to design careful experiments that rule out simpler explanations.

My overall view is that these models have learned something genuinely impressive about the statistics of images and language, but I don't see strong evidence that they've built the kind of causal, compositional world models that humans use to understand and reason about what they see.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it sees no strong evidence that these models have built causal, compositional world models, and contrasts their behavior with causal understanding.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses testing models and their limitations but does not identify whether different learning methods or training data could lead to causal models as an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say the first thing I try to do is be very careful about what we mean by "causal model," because that phrase gets thrown around a lot. When people see something like DALL-E or one of these text-to-image systems produce a picture of, say, a cat sitting on a stack of books, there's a temptation to say, "Look, it understands what cats are, what books are, what 'on top of' means." But producing a plausible image is not the same thing as having a model of why the world looks the way it does.

So the way I think about assessing it is: you have to probe the system in ways that would distinguish genuine understanding of causal structure from very sophisticated statistical pattern matching. And the key tool for that is systematic variation. You don't just ask whether it can produce the cat on the books. You ask whether it can handle "the books on the cat," or "a cat under a transparent table," or situations that require understanding support, gravity, containment, occlusion. These are the kinds of intuitive physics concepts that even very young children have. And what we find, when people have done these kinds of studies, is that the models are often quite brittle. They'll get the common configurations right because those appear frequently in the training data, and they'll fail on the compositional or counterfactual cases.

I think that's really the crux of it. A causal model should let you reason about counterfactuals, about what would happen if something were different. If a system has only learned correlations between text tokens and pixel patterns, it can interpolate beautifully within the distribution it's seen, but it won't generalize to novel combinations in a principled way. And the failures we see are telling: wrong numbers of objects, spatial relations that get scrambled, attributes that bind to the wrong object. A system that actually understood that "a red cube on a blue sphere" involves two distinct objects with distinct properties and a physical relation between them wouldn't make those kinds of errors.

There's also an evaluation problem that I think the field hasn't fully grappled with. Many of the benchmarks we use are themselves drawn from the same distributions the models are trained on, so good performance can be contaminated by memorization or by shortcuts the models have found. I'm very much in favor of the approach that cognitive scientists have used for decades: design controlled experiments where you know what the right answer is, you know what a shortcut answer would look like, and you can tell the difference. We've done some of this work on abstraction and analogy, and I think the same methodology applies to grounding and causality in multimodal models.

So my honest assessment is that these systems have learned something genuinely impressive about the statistical structure linking language and visual appearance. But I'm skeptical that they've learned causal models in the sense of understanding how objects and forces and agents interact in the world. The burden of proof should be on the claim of understanding, and the way to meet that burden is through adversarial, systematic testing rather than through impressive demos.

r001.rationale: The response says it is skeptical that current text-image systems have learned causal models, describing their abilities as statistical learning and their errors as evidence of brittle reasoning.

r002.rationale: The response discusses testing and benchmark limitations, but does not identify whether different learning methods or training data could enable causal models as an open question.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by a causal model. A system can learn very rich statistical associations between images and text without necessarily understanding how things in the world cause other things to happen. And it can be hard to distinguish those just by looking at impressive examples of what it generates.

What I would want to do is test it in situations where those two possibilities make different predictions. Can it predict what happens when you intervene—when you change something in a scene? Can it distinguish a change that actually affects the outcome from one that’s merely correlated with it? And can it do that in a novel situation, where it can’t simply reproduce a familiar pattern?

For example, if you remove the support underneath an object, can it consistently predict what happens, even when you vary the objects and the setting? Getting one example right wouldn’t tell us very much. You’d want systematic tests across lots of variations.

So I wouldn’t say that learning from text and images rules out learning something causal. But the fact that a model produces a convincing image or a plausible explanation isn’t, by itself, evidence that it has a robust causal model of the world. That’s something we have to investigate much more carefully.

r001.rationale: The response says text–image learning does not necessarily produce causal understanding and that the evidence is insufficient; it does not express the view that these models are not developing causal models.

r002.rationale: It says text–image learning does not rule out causal learning, but does not identify different learning methods or training data as an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by a causal model. A system can learn very rich statistical associations between images and text without understanding what causes what in the world. And producing a plausible image or a convincing explanation doesn’t, by itself, distinguish those possibilities.

One way to probe that is to ask what happens when you intervene. If you change one aspect of a scene, can the system predict the consequences, including what should stay the same? Can it do that in a situation that’s different from the examples it was trained on? You’d want controlled experiments where familiar correlations come apart, so that simply relying on those correlations gives you the wrong answer.

And I wouldn’t draw a strong conclusion from a few impressive examples—or a few failures. We need systematic tests, with variations that let us understand how the system arrived at its answer. These models clearly learn a lot about the structure of the world. The harder question is whether that knowledge supports robust causal reasoning, and I don’t think fluent language or realistic images alone settle that.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes statistical association from causal understanding, but leaves open whether these models support robust causal reasoning; it does not state that they are not developing causal models.

r002.rationale: The response calls causal reasoning an open question but does not identify different learning methods or training data as possible paths to causal models.
